items.prompt: What is a client-side cache, in the context of this unit?
choices: A local copy of data already fetched from the server, reused on a later request instead of fetching again
A server-side store of session tokens, synced before every request
A browser setting that blocks all network requests until manually refreshed
A full backup of the application's source code
items.explanation: A cache remembers what was already fetched so a later request for the same data can reuse it instead of re-asking the server for something that hasn't changed.
items.reference: Cache — a remembered copy of a prior response, reused instead of re-fetched.
items.reflection: Think of something you kept trusting after it had already changed — a saved phone number, a memorized price — and what finally made you re-check it. How would an app need to know to do the same thing automatically?

items.prompt: What does "cache invalidation" mean?
choices: Deleting the entire cache permanently
Marking cached data as no longer trustworthy, so the next read fetches fresh data instead of serving the stale copy
A configuration flag that disables caching app-wide
Encrypting cached data at rest
items.explanation: Invalidation marks one cached entry as stale because the underlying data changed, so the next read goes to the server instead of reusing outdated data.
items.reference: Cache — a remembered copy of a prior response, reused instead of re-fetched.
items.reflection: Think of something you kept trusting after it had already changed — a saved phone number, a memorized price — and what finally made you re-check it. How would an app need to know to do the same thing automatically?

items.prompt: A news site caches its homepage article list. An editor fixes a typo in the top headline, but the write path never touches the cached homepage entry, and the cache has no expiry. What will a reader who already loaded the homepage see on their next visit?
choices: The corrected headline immediately
The old, uncorrected headline — the cache still holds it and nothing invalidated it
A blank homepage, since mismatched data blocks rendering
An error page
items.explanation: A cache only stops serving stale data once something tells it to. Here nothing did, so it keeps confidently returning the outdated headline indefinitely — the bug is a missing invalidation step, not a broken cache.
items.reference: Cache — a remembered copy of a prior response, reused instead of re-fetched.
items.reflection: Think of something you kept trusting after it had already changed — a saved phone number, a memorized price — and what finally made you re-check it. How would an app need to know to do the same thing automatically?

items.prompt: A cache entry is invalidated the instant a write succeeds, but the next read of that key doesn't happen until a few seconds later. What should a correctly built cache do with that key in the meantime?
choices: Keep serving the old value until a read actually happens to trigger re-fetching
Treat the key as untrustworthy immediately, so whenever the next read does happen, it fetches fresh data instead of reusing the old value
Delete the entire cache, not just that key
Nothing — invalidation only matters if a read is already in progress
items.explanation: Invalidation's effect is on the next read, not on some idle background timer — marking the key stale now means whenever it's next read, fresh data is fetched instead of the outdated copy.
items.reference: Cache — a remembered copy of a prior response, reused instead of re-fetched.

items.prompt: Why does revisiting a page that re-fetches the same unchanged data over and over waste effort?
choices: Because each fetch re-requests data that likely hasn't changed, when a cached copy could have been reused instead
Because any network fetch at all is considered a bug
Because browsers cap the total number of fetches per session
Because servers bill extra for repeated identical requests
items.explanation: If the underlying data hasn't changed, re-fetching it is redundant work — a cache lets the page reuse what it already retrieved instead of asking again.

items.prompt: What's the risk of a cache that is never invalidated after the underlying data changes?
choices: None — a cache re-checks itself against the server on a fixed schedule automatically
It will keep serving outdated data indefinitely, actively misleading the UI
The application will crash the next time that value is read
The cache empties itself the first time it's read
items.explanation: Without invalidation, a cache has no way to know its data is outdated — it keeps serving the stale copy forever, which is worse than simply being redundant.

items.prompt: A to-do app fetches the task list once, then reuses that same list for the next three visits without asking the server again. What is the app doing?
choices: Caching
Rolling back
Invalidating
Revalidating
items.explanation: Reusing a previously fetched response instead of re-requesting it is exactly what caching is.

items.prompt: What is a "cache key" used for?
choices: Identifying which cached answer is being read or invalidated, such as `tasks`
Encrypting the cached data
Measuring how long a request took
Authenticating the user
items.explanation: A cache key is the name the app uses to find or invalidate one specific cached entry, like `tasks` or `task:1`.

items.prompt: True or false: once data is cached, it's safe to assume it stays correct forever.
choices: True — caching guarantees correctness
False — cached data can go stale the moment the underlying data changes, which is why invalidation exists
True, but only for text data
False, but only on mobile devices
items.explanation: A cache is only as correct as the last time it was refreshed or invalidated — nothing about caching itself keeps data correct over time.

items.prompt: A shopping page caches its product list, and a product's price changes on the server. If nothing invalidates the cached price, what happens on the next page view?
choices: The old price keeps showing, because the cache doesn't know anything changed
The new price shows automatically, because caches always detect server-side changes
The page crashes
The cache clears itself automatically every hour
items.explanation: A cache has no built-in awareness of server-side changes — without an explicit invalidation step, it keeps serving the price it already has.

items.prompt: What problem is caching specifically designed to avoid?
choices: Re-fetching data that almost certainly hasn't changed since the last fetch
Writing data to the server
Running JavaScript too slowly
Showing a loading spinner
items.explanation: Caching's entire point is skipping redundant reads of data that hasn't changed — it isn't a fix for slow writes or slow code.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the purpose of each mechanism?
choices: Caching avoids redundant fetches; invalidation avoids serving outdated data
Caching avoids outdated data; invalidation avoids redundant fetches
Both avoid the exact same problem
Neither relates to fetching data
items.explanation: Caching skips a fetch that would return the same result; invalidation is what stops that same fetch-skipping from eventually serving data that's wrong.

items.prompt: What does "stale-while-revalidate" mean?
choices: Blocking the UI until a fresh server response arrives, every time
Showing the cached (possibly outdated) data immediately, while a fresh request runs in the background to update it
Deleting old data from the cache the moment it becomes outdated
Refusing to display any cached data older than one second
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate shows the cached data right away for an instant response, then quietly checks the server in the background and updates the UI if the fresh response differs.
items.reference: SWR — show cached data instantly, confirm (and correct) in the background.
items.reflection: Stale-while-revalidate trades a moment of possible wrongness for never making someone wait. Where else in life do you accept a slightly-out-of-date answer now over a guaranteed-correct answer later — and where would that trade be a bad idea?

items.prompt: In stale-while-revalidate, what happens if the background re-fetch finds the data actually changed?
choices: Nothing — the UI keeps showing the original cached version forever
The cache is updated and the UI is updated to reflect the fresh data
The application throws an unrecoverable error
The user is logged out automatically
items.explanation: If the background fetch's result differs from what was cached, the cache is updated and the UI reflects the corrected data — the user briefly saw stale data, then it self-corrected.
items.reference: SWR — show cached data instantly, confirm (and correct) in the background.
items.reflection: Stale-while-revalidate trades a moment of possible wrongness for never making someone wait. Where else in life do you accept a slightly-out-of-date answer now over a guaranteed-correct answer later — and where would that trade be a bad idea?

items.prompt: A weather app shows yesterday's cached forecast instantly on open, then quietly checks for a fresh one in the background. A storm warning was added an hour ago. What does the user see, and when?
choices: The storm warning instantly, because stale-while-revalidate never shows outdated data
Yesterday's forecast first, then the storm warning once the background check resolves and finds a difference
Nothing at all until the background check finishes
The storm warning only after the user manually refreshes
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate always shows the cached answer first, by design — the storm warning only appears once the background revalidation completes and the UI is corrected.

items.prompt: A live stock-price ticker is built with stale-while-revalidate, showing the last cached price instantly on every page load. Is this a good fit for the pattern?
choices: Yes, because stale-while-revalidate is always the fastest option for any data
No — a live price changes constantly, so briefly showing a stale number before correcting it may be exactly the wrong trade for this data
Yes, because the background fetch guarantees the stale price is never actually shown
No, because stale-while-revalidate cannot be used for numeric data
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate always shows the cached value first by design — for data where even brief staleness is unacceptable, like a live price, that's the wrong trade-off, not a bug in the pattern itself.
items.reference: SWR — show cached data instantly, confirm (and correct) in the background.
items.reflection: Stale-while-revalidate trades a moment of possible wrongness for never making someone wait. Where else in life do you accept a slightly-out-of-date answer now over a guaranteed-correct answer later — and where would that trade be a bad idea?

items.prompt: What's shown to the user the instant stale-while-revalidate runs, before any network request completes?
choices: A blank loading screen
The previously cached data, even if it might be a little outdated
An error message
Nothing, until the background fetch finishes
items.explanation: The whole point of the pattern is showing the cached answer immediately instead of making the user wait for a network round trip first.

items.prompt: If the background re-fetch in stale-while-revalidate finds the data is unchanged, what does the user see?
choices: No visible change — the cached data they were already shown was already correct
A page reload
A brief error flash
The cached data disappears
items.explanation: When the fresh response matches the cached one, there's nothing to correct, so nothing visibly changes.

items.prompt: What is being traded away in exchange for an instant response under stale-while-revalidate?
choices: A guarantee that the very first thing shown is already up to date
Network bandwidth, permanently
The ability to ever show fresh data at all
Nothing is traded away
items.explanation: The pattern deliberately shows a possibly-stale answer first — it trades a brief window of possible staleness for never blocking on the network.

items.prompt: Why is stale-while-revalidate a poor fit for a live account balance shown during an active money transfer?
choices: Because even a few seconds of staleness could show an incorrect balance at a moment where accuracy matters most
Because balances can't technically be cached at all
Because it would make the transfer itself fail
Because background requests aren't allowed during transfers
items.explanation: The pattern always shows a possibly-stale value first — fine for most data, risky for a number someone needs to trust as current right now.

items.prompt: What two things happen, in order, under stale-while-revalidate on a cache hit?
choices: Show the cached value immediately, then check the server in the background
Check the server first, then show whatever it returns
Delete the cache, then fetch fresh data
Show an error, then retry
items.explanation: A cache hit returns the stored value right away; the background revalidation happens afterward, not before.

items.prompt: Does stale-while-revalidate mean the user never sees outdated data?
choices: No — it means they may see outdated data briefly, then get corrected automatically
Yes — the pattern guarantees the first render is always correct
Yes, as long as the network is fast
No — it means they always see an error instead
items.explanation: The pattern's name says it plainly: the cached data is allowed to be stale while it's being revalidated — staleness is part of the design, not something it eliminates.

items.prompt: A help-documentation page rarely changes. Is stale-while-revalidate a reasonable fit for it?
choices: Yes — brief staleness on rarely-changing content is low-risk, and the instant load is a clear win
No — documentation pages can never be cached
No — only numeric data can use this pattern
Yes, but only if the page has fewer than 100 words
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate fits best exactly where this unit's scenario lives: data where a brief window of possible staleness costs little, in exchange for never blocking on the network.

items.prompt: What triggers the UI to update under stale-while-revalidate, after the cached value was already shown?
choices: The background fetch resolving and its result differing from the cached value
A fixed timer that always fires after exactly one second
The user manually clicking refresh
The server pushing an update over a websocket, required by the pattern
items.explanation: The update is driven by comparing the background fetch's result to what was cached — if they differ, the UI is corrected; if not, nothing changes.

items.prompt: What is an "optimistic update"?
choices: Updating the UI immediately as if a write request already succeeded, without waiting for the server's response first
A server-side setting that automatically approves every incoming write
Waiting for two separate server confirmations before updating the UI
A scheduled database backup taken before every write
items.explanation: An optimistic update shows the assumed post-write result immediately, before the server has actually confirmed it — the UI reflects the user's intent right away instead of waiting on the round trip.
items.reference: Optimistic update — show the assumed result now; confirm with the server after.
items.reflection: An optimistic update bets that a request will succeed and shows the result before knowing for sure. What's a non-technical example of acting on an assumption before it's confirmed — and what made it safe (or not) to do?

items.prompt: Why does an optimistic update make a checkbox feel faster, even though the server still takes the same 800ms to respond?
choices: Because it reduces the actual network round-trip time to under 800ms
Because the UI shows the result of the click immediately, instead of waiting for the 800ms round trip before showing anything
Because it skips sending the request to the server until the user confirms it
Because it pre-fetches the server's response before the click happens
items.explanation: The network timing doesn't change — what changes is when the UI shows the result relative to when the server confirms it.

choices: Nothing else — optimistic updates are complete on their own
A way to undo the optimistic comment and tell the user it was rejected, once the server's real answer arrives
A way to prevent the server from ever rejecting a comment
A second, slower confirmation screen before any comment is ever shown
items.explanation: An optimistic update only covers the "assume success" half — the comment box also needs a way to react when that assumption turns out to be wrong, which is exactly what a rollback is for.

items.prompt: A "like" button turns blue the instant it's clicked, before the server confirms the like was saved. If the app has no network connection at all at that moment, what does an optimistic update, by itself, guarantee about the final state?
choices: That the like is guaranteed to be saved, since the UI already shows it as liked
Nothing on its own — the UI shows the assumed state, but whether it's eventually corrected depends on whether a rollback path actually runs
That the request will automatically succeed once connection returns
That the button will revert to gray within exactly one second
items.explanation: An optimistic update is only the "show the assumed result immediately" half of the mechanism — by itself it makes no promise about correcting a failure; that promise comes from whatever rollback logic is (or isn't) wired up alongside it.

items.prompt: When does an optimistic update show its result, relative to the server's confirmation?
choices: Before the server has confirmed anything
Only after the server confirms
Only if the server rejects the write
Exactly halfway through the request
items.explanation: That's the defining trait of an optimistic update — it shows the assumed result immediately, ahead of confirmation.

items.prompt: A checkbox app waits for the server's response before showing a check mark. Is this an optimistic update?
choices: No — waiting for confirmation first is the opposite of an optimistic update
Yes, as long as the server responds quickly
Yes, because any UI change counts as optimistic
No, because checkboxes can never be optimistic
items.explanation: An optimistic update specifically shows the result before confirmation — waiting for the server first is the naive, non-optimistic approach.

items.prompt: What does an optimistic update assume about the write it just triggered?
choices: That it will succeed
That it will definitely fail
That the user will cancel it
That the server is offline
items.explanation: "Optimistic" means assuming success — the UI shows the result that would be true if the write succeeds.

items.prompt: Does an optimistic update change how long the server actually takes to respond?
choices: No — the server's response time is unchanged; only when the UI shows a result changes
Yes — it always makes the server respond faster
Yes — it skips the server round trip entirely
No — but it doubles the server's response time
items.explanation: The network timing is identical either way — the optimistic version just stops making the user wait for it before reacting.

items.prompt: A "save" button on a text editor instantly shows "Saved" the moment it's clicked, before the save request even finishes. What is this an example of?
choices: An optimistic update
A rollback
A cache invalidation
A stale-while-revalidate read
items.explanation: Showing the assumed post-write result ("Saved") before the write is actually confirmed is exactly what an optimistic update does.

items.prompt: Why is the user's "intent" relevant to optimistic updates?
choices: Because the user's intent (what they clicked) is already known the instant they click, so the UI can reflect it without waiting
Because the server needs to guess the user's intent from network data
Because intent is unrelated to optimistic updates
Because intent only matters for caching, not writes
items.explanation: The app already knows what the user wants the instant they click — an optimistic update simply reflects that known intent immediately rather than delaying it.

items.prompt: Does caching (as covered earlier in this unit) solve the same problem as an optimistic update?
choices: No — caching is about reusing read data; optimistic updates are about not waiting on a write
Yes — they're two names for the same mechanism
Yes, but optimistic updates only work on mobile
No — caching is strictly faster than optimistic updates in every case
items.explanation: Caching speeds up reads by reusing data already fetched; optimistic updates speed up the perceived result of a write by not waiting for confirmation — different directions, different fixes.

items.prompt: If a write is applied optimistically and the server later confirms success, what visibly changes in the UI at that moment?
choices: Nothing — the UI already showed the correct result
The UI reverts and then re-applies the change
A loading spinner appears retroactively
The page reloads
items.explanation: When the server agrees with the optimistic assumption, there's nothing left to correct — the confirmation is a non-event visually.

items.prompt: What is a "rollback" in the context of an optimistic update?
choices: Undoing an optimistic update and restoring the previous UI state, used when the server's actual response is a failure
Restarting the entire application after any failed request
A server-side audit log of every request
Automatically retrying a failed request forever
items.explanation: A rollback restores the UI to its state from before the optimistic change, used when the server later reports the write actually failed or was rejected.
items.reference: Rollback — restore the exact prior state once an optimistic assumption turns out wrong.
items.reflection: A rollback only works if you knew the exact state you were in before you changed it. Where in your own life do you keep a "before" record specifically so you can undo something cleanly if it doesn't work out?

items.prompt: Why does an optimistic update need a rollback path, not just the initial immediate UI update?
choices: Because without it, a failed write leaves the UI showing a false state that never actually happened
Because adding a rollback path makes the initial optimistic update happen faster
Because servers require a rollback path by specification
Rollbacks are optional and rarely needed once caching is in place
items.explanation: If the server rejects the write and nothing rolls back the optimistic change, the UI keeps showing a state that never actually happened — actively misleading, not just delayed.

items.prompt: An optimistic "like" button turns blue immediately, and the server later rejects the like. Instead of restoring an exact snapshot, the app just re-fetches the whole post from the server to decide what to show. What's the risk with that approach, compared to using a snapshot?
choices: There's no risk — re-fetching and snapshotting always produce the identical result
The re-fetch reflects whatever the server currently has, which may include other changes made in the meantime — it can revert more than just the failed like
Re-fetching is always slower than failing silently, so it should never be used
Re-fetching makes the rollback happen before the optimistic update, which is impossible
items.explanation: A snapshot restores exactly the state from right before the optimistic change. A re-fetch instead asks for "whatever is true now," which can include unrelated changes made in between — rolling back to it can undo more than intended.
items.reference: Rollback — restore the exact prior state once an optimistic assumption turns out wrong.

items.prompt: A rollback restores the checkbox's visual state after a failed write, but the code that triggered the rollback never tells the rest of the app that anything went wrong. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — restoring the visual state is the entire job of a rollback
The failure still needs to be surfaced (e.g. an error shown, logged, or re-thrown) — otherwise the rest of the program never learns the write failed, even though the pixels are correct again
The rollback should have shown the optimistic state for longer before reverting
The server should be blamed publicly for the failure
items.explanation: A rollback that only fixes what's visually shown but swallows the underlying failure still hides information the caller needed — the UI looks honest again, but the program's own state about what happened is now wrong in a quieter way.

items.prompt: When does a rollback happen?
choices: When the server's response to an optimistic update turns out to be a failure or rejection
Every single time an optimistic update is applied, regardless of outcome
Only when the user manually requests it
Only when the network is completely offline
items.explanation: A rollback is specifically the response to a failed or rejected write — on success, there's nothing to roll back.

items.prompt: What does a rollback restore the UI to?
choices: The exact state it was in before the optimistic change was applied
A completely blank state
Whatever state the server happens to be in right now, regardless of history
A random prior state
items.explanation: A correct rollback uses a snapshot of the exact prior state, not a guess or the server's current (possibly unrelated) state.

items.prompt: What must happen before an optimistic change is applied, so a rollback can later be exact?
choices: The prior state must be snapshotted
The server must be notified in advance
The UI must be hidden
The user must confirm twice
items.explanation: Without a snapshot taken before the change, there's nothing precise to restore to if the write fails.

items.prompt: If a server confirms an optimistic write succeeded, does a rollback happen?
choices: No — rollback only applies to the failure case
Yes, always, regardless of outcome
Yes, but only on mobile
No, because success is impossible with optimistic updates
items.explanation: On success, the optimistic assumption turned out correct, so there's nothing to undo.

items.prompt: Why is "just reload the page" not the same as building a real rollback path?
choices: Because the UI keeps showing the false optimistic state for an unknown period until a reload happens to occur
Because reloading a page is technically impossible
Because reloading is always slower than the original wait
Because reloads always lose unsaved data
items.explanation: Relying on an eventual reload leaves a window where the UI is actively wrong — a deliberate rollback closes that gap immediately instead of hoping something else fixes it later.

items.prompt: An app applies an optimistic update, and the write fails, but the rollback function is never called. What does the user see?
choices: A UI still showing the optimistic (now-false) state, with no indication anything went wrong
An automatic correction to the true state
A forced page reload
The original pre-click state, restored automatically
items.explanation: Without the rollback actually running, nothing corrects the UI — it keeps showing the assumed state even though the server rejected it.

items.prompt: Besides restoring the visual state, what else should a good rollback do?
choices: Surface the failure, so the rest of the program (and ideally the user) learns something actually went wrong
Nothing else is needed
Automatically retry the exact same request forever
Delete the user's account
items.explanation: A rollback that only fixes the pixels but hides the failure from the rest of the program recreates a quieter version of the same "UI is lying" problem.

items.prompt: Is a rollback a fix for caching problems or for optimistic-update problems?
choices: Optimistic-update problems — it's specifically for undoing a write that was shown before it was confirmed
Caching problems — it's how a stale cache entry gets cleared
Both equally
Neither — it's unrelated to this unit's two fixes
items.explanation: Rollback exists to undo the specific risk optimistic updates introduce (assuming success before it's confirmed) — caching's equivalent concern is invalidation, not rollback.

items.prompt: Some users click the checkbox a second time during the 800ms delay in the opening scenario. Why?

items.prompt: L3's failure-mode table warns about caching a GET response and never invalidating it after a related write. Why does this specifically matter once optimistic updates are also involved?
choices: It doesn't — caching and optimistic updates are completely unrelated concerns
An optimistic write can update the UI's local state correctly while a separately cached GET response for the same data still holds the old, un-invalidated value
Optimistic updates automatically invalidate every cache entry across the whole application instantly
Caching prevents optimistic updates from running at all once enabled
items.explanation: A toggled task's local state can be correct immediately from the optimistic update, while a cached list response for that same data (fetched through a different code path) has no way to know it should be considered stale — the two mechanisms need to agree on when data changes.

items.prompt: What does L3's failure-mode table say is the risk of restoring rollback state by re-fetching instead of using a stored snapshot?
choices: A re-fetch after a failure can race with other changes made in the meantime, potentially reverting more than just the failed update
Re-fetching is always meaningfully faster than using a stored snapshot, so there's no real risk
Re-fetching is simply impossible once any optimistic update has already been applied
There's no risk — re-fetching and snapshotting are functionally identical
items.explanation: A snapshot captures the exact prior state at the moment the optimistic change began. A re-fetch instead asks the server for the current state, which may already reflect other changes made in between — reverting to it can undo more than just the one failed update.

items.prompt: Does a single-field boolean toggle need to worry about other concurrent changes landing in between snapshot and rollback?
choices: Not in the simple case L3 builds — but the unit explicitly flags this as a gap once multiple concurrent changes are introduced
Yes, always, even for a single isolated toggle with nothing else in flight
No, this is never a real concern in any scenario
Only if the array has more than 100 items
items.explanation: L3's worked example is deliberately the simplest case — one change, one snapshot — and explicitly calls out that concurrency complicates this.

items.prompt: Why can caching a GET response and never invalidating it after a related write cause a problem, even if the write itself succeeded?
choices: Because the cached response has no way to know the underlying data changed, so it keeps serving the old version regardless of the write's success
Because a successful write always clears every cache automatically
Because GET responses can never be cached in the first place
Because this only happens if the write fails
items.explanation: A write's success doesn't automatically propagate to a separately cached read — they're two mechanisms that have to be explicitly kept in sync.

items.prompt: What's the risk of restoring a failed optimistic update by re-fetching the current server state, instead of using a snapshot taken before the change?
choices: The re-fetch may reflect other changes made in the meantime, so reverting to it could undo more than just the failed update
Re-fetching is always wrong and should never be used for anything
There's no risk; it's exactly equivalent to a snapshot
Re-fetching always returns the same data as the snapshot would have
items.explanation: A snapshot is frozen at one exact moment; a re-fetch asks for "now," which could include unrelated changes that a revert would wrongly undo too.

items.prompt: Does L3 claim the toggle-done pattern generalizes to every kind of optimistic update with no changes needed?
choices: No — it generalizes for the core idea (snapshot, apply, rollback), but concurrent or multi-field changes need more care than a single snapshot provides
Yes — it works identically for any number of concurrent changes
No — the pattern doesn't generalize at all beyond booleans
Yes, as long as the array has fewer than 10 items
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the pattern generalizes in spirit, but the single-snapshot mechanics specifically assume one change at a time — more moving parts need more careful state tracking.

items.prompt: If two optimistic updates to the same task (toggle done, edit title) are both in flight, and the done-toggle succeeds first, what does the title-edit's snapshot (taken before it started) reflect?
choices: The state from before either change — it does NOT know about the done-toggle that landed afterward
The current, fully up-to-date state, automatically
Only the title field, with no information about done at all
It's impossible for a snapshot to exist in this scenario
items.explanation: A snapshot is frozen at the moment it was taken — it has no way to know about changes that complete later, which is exactly the gap L3's extend-it question surfaces.

items.prompt: What keeps L3's actual toggleTaskOptimistic implementation safe for a single in-flight call, even though it doesn't solve the concurrency extension?
choices: It never mutates the original array in place, so each call has its own honest before/after pair to work with
It locks the entire application until the request finishes
It refuses to run more than once per session
It automatically merges all concurrent changes into one request
items.explanation: Immutability is the precondition that makes reasoning about concurrent calls possible at all — it doesn't fully solve concurrent optimistic updates on its own, but without it, even single calls would be unreliable.

items.prompt: Which failure mode does L3's table associate with "applying an optimistic update without ever checking the server's actual response value"?
choices: Assuming the optimistic value is always correct, which skips the case where the server accepts the write but transforms the stored value
The UI never shows anything at all
The cache automatically clears itself
The server rejects every future request
items.explanation: If the server's response is never actually inspected, a case where the server validates/transforms the value before storing it gets silently missed by the optimistic UI.

items.prompt: Why does L3 explicitly invite the reader to "try extending" the worked example with a concurrency question, rather than treating the toggle example as the whole topic?
choices: Because the worked example is one case, not the entire territory — more complex or concurrent scenarios reveal gaps the simple case doesn't surface
Because the toggle example is actually incorrect as written
Because concurrency questions have no real answer
Because the extend-it question is unrelated to optimistic updates
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a single boolean toggle is the simplest possible case — the extend-it question exists specifically to show the pattern's limits once more realistic complexity (concurrent changes) is introduced.
